papers.topic: States of Matter and Kinetic Theory
papers.title: States of Matter and Kinetic Theory: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on states of matter and kinetic theory, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In the smoke-cell experiment, the smoke particles are seen to move randomly because
questions.explanation:
Brownian motion: invisible air molecules bombard each smoke particle unevenly, pushing it first one way and then another.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- they are alive: Smoke particles are not living; the motion is caused by collisions.
- convection currents carry them about: The motion is a random jiggle in all directions, not a steady current.
- they are attracted by the light: Light is used only to make the particles visible.

options.label: A
options.content: they are struck unevenly by fast-moving air molecules

options.label: D
options.content: they are attracted by the light

questions.stem: Which statement about the particles of a gas is correct?
questions.explanation:
Gas particles have large spaces between them and move fast and randomly, so gases fill their containers and are easily compressed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- They vibrate about fixed positions.  
  That describes the particles of a solid.
- They are closely packed in a regular pattern.  
  That describes a crystalline solid.
- They are close together and slide past one another.  
  That describes a liquid.

options.label: A
options.content: They are far apart and move rapidly in random directions.

options.label: C
options.content: They are closely packed in a regular pattern.

options.label: D
options.content: They are close together and slide past one another.

questions.stem: Diffusion takes place fastest in
questions.explanation:
Gas particles are far apart and fast, so they mix most quickly.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- liquids: Liquid particles are closer together and move more slowly than gas particles.
- solids: Diffusion in solids is extremely slow.
- all states equally: The rate depends on how freely and how fast the particles move.

questions.stem: Evaporation causes cooling because
questions.explanation:
Losing the fastest molecules lowers the average kinetic energy, and therefore the temperature, of the liquid left behind.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the liquid gives out heat to the surroundings: Evaporation takes in heat; the cooling comes from losing fast molecules.
- the slowest molecules escape from the liquid: Only molecules with enough energy can escape: the fastest ones.
- the liquid's mass increases: Evaporation reduces the mass of the liquid.

options.label: A
options.content: the most energetic molecules escape from the liquid

options.label: B
options.content: the liquid gives out heat to the surroundings

options.label: C
options.content: the slowest molecules escape from the liquid

questions.stem: Which of the following is a difference between evaporation and boiling?
questions.explanation:
Evaporation: any temperature, at the surface, slow. Boiling: fixed temperature, throughout the liquid, rapid.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Evaporation occurs throughout the liquid; boiling only at the surface.  
  It is the other way round: evaporation is a surface process.
- Boiling causes cooling; evaporation does not.  
  Evaporation causes cooling; during boiling the temperature stays constant.
- Evaporation needs a flame; boiling does not.  
  Evaporation happens without any flame, e.g. clothes drying.

options.label: A
options.content: Evaporation occurs at all temperatures; boiling occurs at a fixed temperature.

options.label: B
options.content: Evaporation occurs throughout the liquid; boiling only at the surface.

options.label: C
options.content: Boiling causes cooling; evaporation does not.

options.label: D
options.content: Evaporation needs a flame; boiling does not.

questions.stem: According to the kinetic theory, the temperature of a gas is a measure of
questions.explanation:
The faster the molecules move on average, the higher the temperature.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the number of molecules present: More molecules do not mean a higher temperature.
- the size of its molecules: Molecular size does not set the temperature.
- the potential energy of its molecules: Temperature is linked to the motion (kinetic energy) of the molecules.

options.label: C
options.content: the potential energy of its molecules

options.label: D
options.content: the average kinetic energy of its molecules

questions.stem: Water wets clean glass because
questions.explanation:
When adhesion to the glass exceeds the attraction between water molecules, the water spreads over the glass.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the cohesion of water is greater than its adhesion to glass: That is why mercury does not wet glass.
- water is denser than glass: Glass is denser than water, and density does not decide wetting.
- glass absorbs water: Glass does not absorb water.

options.label: A
options.content: the adhesion between water and glass is greater than the cohesion of water

options.label: B
options.content: the cohesion of water is greater than its adhesion to glass

questions.stem: Which of these is an amorphous solid?
questions.explanation:
Glass has an irregular particle arrangement and softens over a range of temperatures instead of melting sharply.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- common salt: Salt forms crystals with a regular lattice.
- ice: Ice is crystalline.
- copper: Metals are crystalline.

papers.title: Elasticity and Hooke's Law: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on elasticity and hooke's law, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A spring of natural length 15 cm stretches to 18 cm when a load of 6 N hangs on it. What is its spring constant?
questions.explanation:
$e = 18 - 15 = 3\ \text{cm} = 0.03\ \text{m}$; $k = \dfrac{F}{e} = \dfrac{6}{0.03} = 200\ \text{N m}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2 N m⁻¹: You used the extension in centimetres. 3 cm = 0.03 m.
- 33.3 N m⁻¹: You used the stretched length (18 cm) instead of the extension.
- 40 N m⁻¹: You used the natural length instead of the extension.

questions.stem: A spring obeys Hooke's law and extends by 2 cm under a load of 5 N. What load extends it by 7 cm?
questions.explanation:
$F \propto e$: $F = 5 \times \dfrac{7}{2} = 17.5\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.43 N: You inverted the proportion: load is directly proportional to extension.
- 35 N: You multiplied 5 by 7 without dividing by 2.
- 2.8 N: You divided the extensions the wrong way round.

questions.stem: Hooke's law states that the extension of a spring is proportional to the load, provided
questions.explanation:
Beyond the elastic limit (strictly, the limit of proportionality) extension is no longer proportional to load.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the spring is made of steel: Hooke's law applies to many elastic materials, not only steel.
- the load is applied quickly: The speed of loading is not part of the law.
- the spring is horizontal: Orientation does not matter.

options.label: A
options.content: the elastic limit is not exceeded

options.label: B
options.content: the spring is made of steel

questions.stem: How much energy is stored in a spring of spring constant 400 N m⁻¹ when it is stretched by 0.05 m?
questions.explanation:
$E = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 400 \times 0.05^2 = 0.5\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1 J: You forgot the ½ in $\tfrac{1}{2}ke^2$.
- 10 J: You used $\tfrac{1}{2}ke$ without squaring the extension.
- 20 J: That is the force, $ke$, not the energy.

questions.stem: A wire of cross-sectional area 2 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries a tension of 80 N. What is the tensile stress?
questions.explanation:
Stress $= \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{80}{2 \times 10^{-6}} = 4 \times 10^{7}\ \text{Pa}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.4 × 10⁷ Pa: Check the power of ten: 80 ÷ (2 × 10⁻⁶) = 4 × 10⁷ Pa.
- 8 × 10⁷ Pa: You divided by 10⁻⁶ instead of 2 × 10⁻⁶.
- 40 × 10⁷ Pa: That would be 4 × 10⁸ Pa, ten times too large.

questions.stem: The unit of tensile strain is
questions.explanation:
Strain = extension ÷ original length, a ratio of two lengths, so it has no unit.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- N m⁻²: That is the unit of stress.
- N m⁻¹: That is the unit of the spring constant.
- m: Strain is extension divided by original length: the metres cancel.

questions.stem: Two identical springs each extend 4 cm under a load of 10 N. How far does a 10 N load stretch the two springs joined end to end (in series)?
questions.explanation:
In series each spring carries the whole load and extends 4 cm: total 8 cm.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4 cm: Each spring carries the full 10 N, so both stretch 4 cm.
- 2 cm: That is the extension for the springs side by side (in parallel).
- 16 cm: You doubled twice.

questions.stem: A material that breaks suddenly with little or no plastic deformation is described as
questions.explanation:
Brittle materials such as glass and cast iron snap without stretching much.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ductile: Ductile materials stretch a lot (plastically) before breaking.
- elastic: An elastic material returns to its shape; this does not describe breaking.
- malleable: Malleable materials can be hammered into sheets.

papers.title: Surface Tension, Capillarity, and Viscosity: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on surface tension, capillarity, and viscosity, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A dry needle placed gently on water floats because of
questions.explanation:
The water surface acts like a stretched skin that can support the light needle.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- upthrust alone: Steel is denser than water; upthrust alone cannot support it.
- viscosity: Viscosity resists motion through a fluid; it does not support a resting needle.
- capillarity: Capillarity is the rise of a liquid in narrow tubes.

questions.stem: Which of the following reduces the surface tension of water?
questions.explanation:
Soap and detergents (and raising the temperature) lower surface tension.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- cooling the water: Cooling increases surface tension slightly; heating reduces it.
- placing a needle on it: A needle does not change the surface tension.
- increasing the depth of water: Depth does not affect surface tension.

questions.stem: In narrow glass tubes dipped in water, the water rises highest in the tube that is
questions.explanation:
The narrower the tube, the higher the capillary rise.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- widest: Capillary rise is greater in narrower tubes.
- longest: The length of the tube does not decide the rise.
- made of plastic: Water rises because it wets glass; the question compares glass tubes.

questions.stem: The meniscus of mercury in a glass tube is
questions.explanation:
Mercury's cohesion exceeds its adhesion to glass, so its surface curves down and it is depressed in a narrow tube.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- concave, and the mercury rises above the outside level: That describes water in glass.
- flat, and the level is unchanged: Mercury's cohesion gives a curved surface.
- concave, and the mercury is depressed: Mercury's surface curves downwards at the edges (convex).

options.label: A
options.content: convex, and the mercury is depressed below the outside level

options.label: B
options.content: concave, and the mercury rises above the outside level

options.label: C
options.content: flat, and the level is unchanged

options.label: D
options.content: concave, and the mercury is depressed

questions.stem: Oil rises up the wick of a kerosene lamp by
questions.explanation:
The fine spaces between the wick's fibres act as capillary tubes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- convection: Convection is heat transfer by fluid movement.
- diffusion: Diffusion is too slow and random to lift the oil.
- radiation: Radiation transfers heat, not liquid.

questions.stem: A steel ball falling through glycerine reaches terminal velocity when
questions.explanation:
With the upward forces (upthrust + drag) balancing the weight, the resultant force is zero and the speed is constant.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- its weight equals the viscous drag alone: The upthrust also acts upwards and must be included.
- the viscous drag becomes zero: Drag is greatest at terminal velocity.
- its acceleration equals g: At terminal velocity the acceleration is zero.

options.label: A
options.content: its weight equals the upthrust plus the viscous drag

options.label: B
options.content: its weight equals the viscous drag alone

questions.stem: When engine oil is warmed, its viscosity
questions.explanation:
The viscosity of liquids falls as temperature rises.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increases: Liquids flow more easily when warm; it is gases whose viscosity rises with temperature.
- stays the same: Temperature strongly affects the viscosity of liquids.
- becomes zero: Warm oil still has some viscosity.

questions.stem: A ball of weight 0.50 N falls through a liquid at its terminal velocity. The upthrust on it is 0.08 N. What is the viscous drag?
questions.explanation:
At terminal velocity, $W = U + F$, so $F = 0.50 - 0.08 = 0.42\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.58 N: You added the upthrust to the weight.
- 0.5 N: You left out the upthrust.
- 0.08 N: That is the upthrust, not the drag.

papers.title: Density and Pressure in Fluids: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on density and pressure in fluids, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: What is the pressure due to water at a depth of 8 m? (density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$p = h\rho g = 8 \times 1000 \times 10 = 80\,000\ \text{Pa}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 8000 Pa: You left out g (or the density of 1000 kg m⁻³ was used as 100).
- 800 Pa: You used the depth × 100.
- 180000 Pa: You added atmospheric pressure (100 000 Pa); the question asks for the pressure due to the water.

questions.stem: A box of weight 600 N rests on a face of area 0.3 m². What pressure does it exert on the floor?
questions.explanation:
$p = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{600}{0.3} = 2000\ \text{Pa}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 180 Pa: You multiplied the weight by the area.
- 0.0005 Pa: You divided the area by the weight.
- 200 Pa: You divided by 3 instead of 0.3.

questions.stem: The pressure at a point in a liquid does NOT depend on
questions.explanation:
$p = h\rho g$ depends only on depth, density and g, not on the container's shape or width.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the depth of the point: Pressure increases with depth ($p = h\rho g$).
- the density of the liquid: Denser liquids give more pressure at the same depth.
- the acceleration due to gravity: $g$ appears in $p = h\rho g$.

questions.stem: Mercury rather than water is used in a barometer mainly because
questions.explanation:
A water barometer would need a column about 10 m tall; mercury (RD 13.6) needs only about 0.76 m.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- it is cheaper than water: Mercury is far more expensive than water.
- it does not stick to glass: That helps, but the main reason is its high density.
- it is a good conductor of heat: That matters for thermometers, not barometers.

options.label: A
options.content: its high density gives a short, convenient column

options.label: C
options.content: it does not stick to glass

options.label: D
options.content: it is a good conductor of heat

questions.stem: A stone weighs 6.0 N in air and 4.0 N when fully immersed in water. What is its relative density?
questions.explanation:
Upthrust $= 6.0 - 4.0 = 2.0$ N. $\text{RD} = \dfrac{6.0}{2.0} = 3$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.5: You divided the weight in air by the weight in water. Divide by the upthrust (loss in weight).
- 2: That is the upthrust in newtons.
- 0.33: You divided the upthrust by the weight.

questions.stem: Archimedes' principle states that a body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to
questions.explanation:
Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced, whether the body floats or sinks.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the weight of the body: That equals the upthrust only for a floating body (law of flotation).
- the volume of the fluid displaced: Upthrust is a force, equal to the weight of displaced fluid, not its volume.
- the density of the fluid: Density alone is not a force.

options.label: B
options.content: the weight of the fluid displaced

options.label: C
options.content: the volume of the fluid displaced

questions.stem: A block of wood of density 700 kg m⁻³ floats in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. What fraction of its volume is submerged?
questions.explanation:
Weight of block = weight of water displaced: $700V = 1000V_{sub}$, so $\dfrac{V_{sub}}{V} = 0.7$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.3: That is the fraction above the water.
- 1.43: You inverted the ratio; the fraction must be less than 1.
- 0.5: The fraction submerged equals the ratio of the densities, 700/1000.

questions.stem: In a hydraulic press, a force of 50 N is applied to a piston of area 10 cm². What force acts on the large piston of area 400 cm²?
questions.explanation:
$F_2 = F_1\dfrac{A_2}{A_1} = 50 \times \dfrac{400}{10} = 2000\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.25 N: You divided by the area ratio instead of multiplying.
- 20000 N: You multiplied by 400 alone instead of the ratio 400/10.
- 460 N: You added the areas to the force.

papers.title: Temperature and Thermometers: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on temperature and thermometers, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Convert 57 °C to kelvin.
questions.explanation:
$T = \theta + 273 = 57 + 273 = 330\ \text{K}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 216 K: You subtracted 273 instead of adding (and ignored the sign).
- 57 K: Celsius and kelvin readings differ by 273.
- -216 K: To convert °C to K, add 273.

questions.stem: The mercury thread of an unmarked thermometer is 3 cm long at the ice point and 23 cm long at the steam point. What temperature corresponds to a length of 12 cm?
questions.explanation:
$\theta = \dfrac{12 - 3}{23 - 3} \times 100 = \dfrac{9}{20} \times 100 = 45\ °\text{C}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 60 °C: You used 12 ÷ 20 × 100 without subtracting the 3 cm at the ice point.
- 52.2 °C: You divided by 23 instead of the interval 23 − 3 = 20.
- 9 °C: That is the length above the ice point, not the temperature.

questions.stem: The thermometric property used in a thermocouple is
questions.explanation:
A thermocouple produces an e.m.f. that depends on the temperature difference between its two junctions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the expansion of a liquid: That is the property of a liquid-in-glass thermometer.
- the resistance of a platinum wire: That is used in a resistance thermometer.
- the pressure of a gas at constant volume: That is used in a constant-volume gas thermometer.

options.label: B
options.content: the resistance of a platinum wire

options.label: C
options.content: the e.m.f. produced at the junction of two different metals

options.label: D
options.content: the pressure of a gas at constant volume

questions.stem: The constriction in a clinical thermometer
questions.explanation:
The constriction breaks the mercury thread when the thermometer cools, so the reading stays until it is shaken back.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- makes the thermometer more sensitive: Sensitivity comes from the narrow bore, not the constriction.
- increases the range of the thermometer: A clinical thermometer has a short range.
- allows the thermometer to be sterilised in boiling water: It would break in boiling water; its range ends near 43 °C.

options.label: B
options.content: increases the range of the thermometer

options.label: C
options.content: allows the thermometer to be sterilised in boiling water

options.label: D
options.content: prevents the mercury from flowing back into the bulb

questions.stem: Alcohol is preferred to mercury in thermometers used in very cold regions because alcohol
questions.explanation:
Alcohol freezes at about −115 °C; mercury freezes at −39 °C.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is opaque: Alcohol is colourless and must be dyed; mercury is the opaque one.
- does not wet glass: Alcohol does wet glass.
- has a higher boiling point: Alcohol boils at only 78 °C.

options.label: A
options.content: has a much lower freezing point

questions.stem: The lower fixed point on the Celsius scale is the temperature of
questions.explanation:
The ice point (0 °C) is the temperature of pure melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- pure water boiling at standard pressure: That is the upper fixed point.
- absolute zero: Absolute zero is −273 °C, not 0 °C.
- a mixture of ice and salt: Salt lowers the melting point of ice.

options.label: A
options.content: pure water boiling at standard pressure

options.label: B
options.content: pure melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure

options.label: D
options.content: a mixture of ice and salt

questions.stem: A resistance thermometer has a resistance of 20 Ω at 0 °C and 28 Ω at 100 °C. What temperature does a resistance of 23 Ω indicate?
questions.explanation:
$\theta = \dfrac{23 - 20}{28 - 20} \times 100 = \dfrac{3}{8} \times 100 = 37.5\ °\text{C}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 82.1 °C: You divided 23 by 28 instead of using the interval between the fixed points.
- 115 °C: You divided 23 by 20, the resistance at 0 °C.
- 3 °C: That is the change in resistance, not the temperature.

questions.stem: Which thermometer is most suitable for measuring the temperature of a furnace?
questions.explanation:
A thermocouple works up to about 1500 °C and responds quickly.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- clinical thermometer: It has a range of only about 35–43 °C.
- alcohol-in-glass thermometer: Alcohol boils at 78 °C.
- mercury-in-glass thermometer: Mercury boils at 357 °C and glass softens far below furnace temperatures.

papers.title: Thermal Expansion: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on thermal expansion, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A brass rod 2.0 m long is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. If the linear expansivity of brass is 2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, what is its increase in length?
questions.explanation:
$\Delta l = \alpha l_0 \Delta\theta = 2 \times 10^{-5} \times 2.0 \times 50 = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 2\ \text{mm}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.002 mm: That is the answer in metres (0.002 m), labelled as millimetres.
- 2.8 mm: You used the final temperature (70 °C) instead of the rise (50 K).
- 1 mm: You used 1 m instead of 2 m.

questions.stem: When a bimetallic strip of brass and iron is heated, it bends so that
questions.explanation:
Brass has the larger expansivity; the longer brass side ends up on the outside of the curve.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the iron is on the outside of the curve: Brass expands more, so it forms the longer, outer side.
- it stays straight but gets longer: The two metals expand by different amounts, so it must bend.
- it twists into a spiral: A straight strip bends into an arc.

options.label: A
options.content: the iron is on the outside of the curve

options.label: B
options.content: it stays straight but gets longer

options.label: D
options.content: the brass is on the outside of the curve

questions.stem: Gaps are left between lengths of railway line in order to
questions.explanation:
Without gaps, rails expanding in the heat would push against each other and buckle.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- allow rainwater to drain: The gaps are for expansion, not drainage.
- reduce the cost of steel: The saving would be negligible.
- make the train run more smoothly: Gaps make the ride slightly less smooth.

options.label: A
options.content: allow for expansion in hot weather

options.label: D
options.content: make the train run more smoothly

questions.stem: The linear expansivity of a metal is 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. What is its cubic (volume) expansivity?
questions.explanation:
$\gamma = 3\alpha = 3 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-5} = 4.5 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹: That is the area expansivity, 2α.
- 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹: That is the linear expansivity itself.
- 0.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹: Volume expansivity is 3α, not α ÷ 3.

questions.stem: Water has its maximum density at
questions.explanation:
Water contracts as it is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C and expands above 4 °C: its density peaks at 4 °C.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0 °C: Water expands as it cools from 4 °C to 0 °C, so it is less dense at 0 °C.
- 100 °C: Water is least dense when hot.
- −4 °C: Below 0 °C pure water is ice, which is less dense than water.

questions.stem: Fish survive in a frozen lake because
questions.explanation:
Ice floats and insulates the water below, which remains liquid at about 4 °C.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- water is densest at 0 °C and sinks: Water is densest at 4 °C; the water at 0 °C stays on top and freezes.
- ice conducts heat well and warms the water: Ice is a poor conductor; that is why it insulates.
- the whole lake stays at 0 °C: The bottom water stays near 4 °C.

options.label: A
options.content: water is densest at 0 °C and sinks

options.label: B
options.content: ice conducts heat well and warms the water

options.label: C
options.content: ice is less dense than water and forms an insulating layer on top

questions.stem: The apparent expansivity of a liquid in a glass vessel is 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ and the cubic expansivity of the glass is 0.3 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. What is the real expansivity of the liquid?
questions.explanation:
$\gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_g = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} + 0.3 \times 10^{-4} = 1.9 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹: You subtracted. Real = apparent + expansivity of the container.
- 0.48 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹: You multiplied the two expansivities.
- 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹: You added 3 × 0.3; the 0.3 × 10⁻⁴ given is already the cubic expansivity.

questions.stem: One end of a steel bridge rests on rollers so that
questions.explanation:
Rollers let the bridge lengthen in the heat and shorten in the cold without cracking its supports.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the bridge can be moved to a new site: The rollers allow small changes in length, not relocation.
- vehicles can cross it faster: Rollers do not affect traffic speed.
- it does not rust: Rollers have nothing to do with rust.

options.label: A
options.content: the bridge can be moved to a new site

options.label: D
options.content: the bridge can expand and contract freely

papers.title: Quantity of Heat and Calorimetry: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on quantity of heat and calorimetry, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 3 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C? (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$Q = mc\Delta\theta = 3 \times 4200 \times 50 = 630\,000\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 882000 J: You used the final temperature (70 °C) instead of the rise (50 K).
- 210000 J: You left out the mass of 3 kg.
- 252000 J: You used the starting temperature (20 °C) as the rise.

questions.stem: The SI unit of specific heat capacity is
questions.explanation:
Specific heat capacity = heat ÷ (mass × temperature change): J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- J K⁻¹: That is the unit of heat capacity (of a whole object).
- J kg⁻¹: That is the unit of specific latent heat.
- J: That is the unit of heat (energy).

questions.stem: 2 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 3 kg of water at 30 °C. What is the final temperature, assuming no heat loss?
questions.explanation:
$2(80 - \theta) = 3(\theta - 30) \Rightarrow 160 - 2\theta = 3\theta - 90 \Rightarrow \theta = 50\ °\text{C}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 55 °C: You averaged the temperatures without weighting by mass.
- 60 °C: You weighted the hot water by 3 kg and the cold by 2 kg.
- 25 °C: You halved the difference between the two temperatures.

questions.stem: A 1.5 kW kettle heats 1.0 kg of water from 25 °C to 100 °C. Ignoring heat loss, how long does this take? (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$t = \dfrac{mc\Delta\theta}{P} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 4200 \times 75}{1500} = 210\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 280 s: You used the final temperature (100 °C) instead of the rise (75 K).
- 3.5 s: That is the time in minutes, not seconds.
- 210000 s: You forgot to change 1.5 kW to 1500 W (you divided by 1.5).

questions.stem: A metal block of mass 2 kg absorbs 18 000 J of heat and its temperature rises by 20 K. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal?
questions.explanation:
$c = \dfrac{Q}{m\Delta\theta} = \dfrac{18\,000}{2 \times 20} = 450\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹: That is the heat capacity of the whole block (J K⁻¹). Divide by the mass too.
- 720000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹: You multiplied instead of dividing.
- 225 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹: You divided by 2 twice.

questions.stem: Water is used to cool car engines mainly because it has a high
questions.explanation:
A high specific heat capacity lets water absorb a lot of heat with only a small temperature rise.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- density: Density does not let it absorb more heat per degree.
- boiling point: Water's boiling point (100 °C) is not especially high.
- thermal conductivity: Water is a poor conductor; its value lies in absorbing heat.

questions.stem: An immersion heater supplies 12 V and 5 A for 2 minutes to 0.6 kg of a liquid, raising its temperature by 4 K. What is the specific heat capacity of the liquid?
questions.explanation:
$c = \dfrac{VIt}{m\Delta\theta} = \dfrac{12 \times 5 \times 120}{0.6 \times 4} = \dfrac{7200}{2.4} = 3000\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 50 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹: You used 2 s instead of 120 s.
- 1800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹: You did not divide by the mass of 0.6 kg.
- 12000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹: You divided by 0.6 × 1 instead of 0.6 × 4.

questions.stem: In a method-of-mixtures experiment, the calorimeter is lagged in order to
questions.explanation:
Lagging (with a poor conductor) reduces heat loss or gain, so 'heat lost = heat gained' holds more closely.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increase the specific heat capacity of the water: Lagging does not change any specific heat capacity.
- make the mixture reach a higher temperature than possible: It only reduces losses; it cannot add heat.
- speed up mixing: Stirring speeds up mixing; lagging reduces heat loss.

options.label: A
options.content: increase the specific heat capacity of the water

options.label: B
options.content: make the mixture reach a higher temperature than possible

options.label: C
options.content: reduce heat exchange with the surroundings

papers.title: Change of State: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on change of state, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C? (specific latent heat of fusion = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$Q = mL_f = 0.5 \times 3.36 \times 10^{5} = 1.68 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 336000 J: You used 1 kg instead of 0.5 kg.
- 672000 J: You multiplied by 2 instead of 0.5.
- 1050 J: You used $mc\Delta\theta$; at 0 °C the ice melts without a temperature change, so use $mL$.

questions.stem: While a pure substance is melting, its temperature
questions.explanation:
Latent heat changes the state without changing the temperature.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- rises steadily: The heat goes into breaking bonds, not into speeding up the particles.
- falls: The substance is gaining heat, not losing it.
- rises and falls: A pure substance melts at one fixed temperature.

questions.stem: How much heat is released when 0.1 kg of steam at 100 °C condenses to water at 100 °C? (L_v = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$Q = mL_v = 0.1 \times 2.26 \times 10^{6} = 2.26 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2260000 J: You used 1 kg instead of 0.1 kg.
- 22600 J: You used 0.01 kg.
- 42000 J: You used $mc\Delta\theta$ with 100 K; condensation at 100 °C needs $mL_v$.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to change 0.2 kg of water at 40 °C completely into steam at 100 °C? (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_v = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
Warm: $0.2 \times 4200 \times 60 = 50\,400$ J. Boil: $0.2 \times 2.26 \times 10^{6} = 452\,000$ J. Total $= 502\,400$ J.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 452000 J: You left out the heat needed to warm the water from 40 °C to 100 °C.
- 50400 J: That only warms the water to 100 °C; it still has to boil.
- 536000 J: You warmed the water through 100 K instead of 60 K.

questions.stem: A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure equals
questions.explanation:
Bubbles of vapour can form and grow only when the vapour pressure matches the pressure pushing on the liquid.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- zero: A liquid with zero vapour pressure would not evaporate at all.
- the pressure at the bottom of the container: Boiling depends on the pressure on the surface.
- its own weight: Weight is not a pressure.

options.label: C
options.content: the pressure at the bottom of the container

questions.stem: Food cooks faster in a pressure cooker because
questions.explanation:
At about twice atmospheric pressure water boils near 120 °C, so food cooks faster.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the pressure lowers the boiling point of water: Higher pressure raises the boiling point.
- steam is a better conductor than water: Steam is a poor conductor.
- the cooker uses less heat: The point is the higher cooking temperature.

options.label: A
options.content: the pressure lowers the boiling point of water

options.label: B
options.content: the higher pressure raises the boiling point of water

options.label: C
options.content: steam is a better conductor than water

questions.stem: In a refrigerator, heat is absorbed from the inside of the cabinet when the refrigerant
questions.explanation:
Evaporating in the freezer coils, the refrigerant takes in latent heat from the inside of the cabinet.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- condenses: Condensation releases heat; it happens in the coils at the back.
- is compressed: Compression heats the vapour; it does not absorb heat from the food.
- freezes: The refrigerant does not freeze in normal operation.

questions.stem: The temperature at which air becomes saturated with water vapour and dew begins to form is called the
questions.explanation:
Cooling air to its dew point makes the water vapour condense as dew, mist or fog.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- boiling point: Boiling point is where a liquid's vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
- melting point: Melting point concerns solid to liquid.
- ice point: The ice point is 0 °C, the melting point of ice.

papers.title: Heat Transfer: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on heat transfer, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth by
questions.explanation:
Only radiation (electromagnetic waves) can travel through a vacuum.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- conduction: Conduction needs a material medium; space is almost empty.
- convection: Convection needs a fluid to move.
- conduction and convection: Neither can cross the vacuum of space.

questions.stem: Which surface is the best absorber of radiant heat?
questions.explanation:
Dull black surfaces are the best absorbers and the best emitters of radiation.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- shiny white: Shiny white surfaces reflect most radiation.
- polished silver: Silvered surfaces are the worst absorbers.
- shiny black: A shiny surface reflects more than a dull one of the same colour.

questions.stem: The heating element of an electric kettle is placed at the bottom so that
questions.explanation:
Water heated at the bottom becomes less dense and rises; cooler water sinks to be heated.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- conduction through the base is reduced: The aim is to heat the water, not to reduce conduction.
- the water heats by radiation: Radiation plays a small part; convection does the work.
- the element stays cool: The element becomes very hot wherever it is placed.

options.label: A
options.content: conduction through the base is reduced

options.label: C
options.content: convection currents can heat all the water

questions.stem: In a vacuum flask, the vacuum between the walls reduces heat transfer by
questions.explanation:
Conduction and convection both need a material medium; a vacuum has none.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- radiation only: Radiation crosses a vacuum; the silvering reduces it.
- radiation and convection: A vacuum does not stop radiation.
- evaporation only: The stopper reduces evaporation.

questions.stem: A sea breeze blows from the sea to the land during the day because
questions.explanation:
Air over the hotter land rises, and cooler air from over the sea flows in to replace it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the sea heats up faster than the land: Water has the higher specific heat capacity, so it warms more slowly.
- cold air rises over the land: Warm, less dense air rises.
- the wind always blows from the sea: At night the breeze reverses (land breeze).

options.label: A
options.content: the land heats up faster, so warm air rises over the land

options.label: B
options.content: the sea heats up faster than the land

options.label: C
options.content: cold air rises over the land

options.label: D
options.content: the wind always blows from the sea

questions.stem: Cooking pots often have wooden or plastic handles because these materials are
questions.explanation:
A poor conductor keeps the handle cool enough to hold.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- good conductors of heat: A good conductor would make the handle too hot to hold.
- good emitters of radiation: Radiation is not the reason for the choice.
- transparent to infrared radiation: That is not the property that matters here.

questions.stem: The greenhouse effect occurs because glass (or carbon dioxide in the atmosphere)
questions.explanation:
Short-wave radiation from the hot Sun passes through; the cooler ground re-emits long-wave infrared, which is trapped.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- lets long-wavelength infrared in but blocks short-wavelength radiation: It is the other way round.
- conducts heat from outside into the greenhouse: Glass is a poor conductor.
- produces heat when sunlight falls on it: Glass does not generate heat; it traps re-emitted infrared.

options.label: A
options.content: lets long-wavelength infrared in but blocks short-wavelength radiation

options.label: B
options.content: conducts heat from outside into the greenhouse

options.label: C
options.content: lets short-wavelength radiation in but traps long-wavelength infrared

options.label: D
options.content: produces heat when sunlight falls on it

questions.stem: Woollen clothing keeps the body warm mainly because
questions.explanation:
Air trapped between the fibres is a very poor conductor, reducing heat loss from the body.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- wool produces heat: Wool does not generate heat.
- wool is a good conductor: A good conductor would carry body heat away.
- wool is a good absorber of sunlight: Clothes keep you warm even indoors at night.

options.label: C
options.content: wool is a good absorber of sunlight

options.label: D
options.content: it traps air, which is a poor conductor

papers.title: Gas Laws: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on gas laws, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 600 cm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. What volume does it occupy at 150 kPa if the temperature is constant?
questions.explanation:
Boyle's law: $p_1V_1 = p_2V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = \dfrac{100 \times 600}{150} = 400\ \text{cm}^3$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 900 cm³: You multiplied by the pressure ratio; volume decreases as pressure increases.
- 1.5 cm³: That is only the ratio of the pressures, 150/100.
- 150 cm³: You confused the pressure with the volume.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 2.0 litres at 27 °C. What volume does it occupy at 127 °C at constant pressure?
questions.explanation:
Charles's law: $V_2 = V_1\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 2.0 \times \dfrac{400}{300} = 2.67\ \text{litres}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 9.41 litres: You used Celsius temperatures; convert to kelvin first.
- 1.5 litres: You inverted the temperature ratio; heating at constant pressure increases the volume.
- 4 litres: You doubled the volume; the absolute temperature rises only from 300 K to 400 K.

questions.stem: The pressure of a fixed mass of gas in a sealed container is 150 kPa at 27 °C. What is its pressure at 87 °C?
questions.explanation:
Pressure law: $p_2 = p_1\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 150 \times \dfrac{360}{300} = 180\ \text{kPa}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 483 kPa: You used Celsius temperatures; use kelvin (300 K and 360 K).
- 125 kPa: You inverted the ratio; heating at constant volume raises the pressure.
- 210 kPa: You added the temperature rise (60) to the pressure.

questions.stem: Boyle's law applies to a fixed mass of gas at constant
questions.explanation:
Boyle's law: pV = constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- pressure: Boyle's law relates pressure and volume, so pressure varies.
- volume: Volume changes in Boyle's law.
- density: Density changes as the volume changes.

questions.stem: A graph of the volume of a fixed mass of gas against its temperature in °C, at constant pressure, is a straight line that cuts the temperature axis at about
questions.explanation:
Extending the graph backwards meets the temperature axis at absolute zero, about −273 °C.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0 °C: At 0 °C the gas still has a large volume.
- −100 °C: Extrapolation of the line reaches the axis at about −273 °C.
- 273 °C: The intercept is below zero, at absolute zero.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C and 100 kPa. What is its volume at 127 °C and 200 kPa?
questions.explanation:
$V_2 = V_1 \times \dfrac{p_1}{p_2} \times \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 300 \times \dfrac{100}{200} \times \dfrac{400}{300} = 200\ \text{cm}^3$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 800 cm³: You used the pressure ratio the wrong way round: doubling the pressure halves the volume.
- 400 cm³: You ignored the change of pressure.
- 150 cm³: You ignored the change of temperature.

questions.stem: According to the kinetic theory, the pressure of a gas in a closed container rises when it is heated because the molecules
questions.explanation:
Faster molecules collide with the walls more frequently and with more force, raising the pressure.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- become larger: Molecules do not grow when heated.
- increase in number: The number of molecules in a sealed container is fixed.
- move more slowly and stick to the walls: Heating makes molecules move faster.

options.label: C
options.content: move faster and hit the walls more often and harder

options.label: D
options.content: move more slowly and stick to the walls

questions.stem: Standard temperature and pressure (s.t.p.) are
questions.explanation:
s.t.p. is 0 °C (273 K) and 760 mmHg (1.01 × 10⁵ Pa).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 298 K and 760 mmHg: 298 K (25 °C) is room temperature, not standard temperature.
- 0 K and 760 mmHg: 0 K is absolute zero.
- 273 K and 1000 mmHg: Standard pressure is 760 mmHg.
